name: Inca religion
info: Inca religion was the polytheist system of beliefs and rites of the Inca Empire, or Tawantinsuyu, which grew out of older Andean traditions and centred on the Sun god Inti, the creator Viracocha, sacred places called wak'a and the worship of royal ancestors.

facts.origin: the Andes, evolving from pre-Inca times into the religion of the Inca Empire, whose state cult was centred on Cusco, where the Inca formed a small city-state in the early 1200s; many origin stories place the beginning of life at Lake Titicaca
facts.founder: none: a body of beliefs and rites that evolved from pre-Inca Andean traditions, most notably those of the Wari, Chavín and Nazca cultures
facts.scriptures: no scriptures are recorded: ritual duties were recorded on quipus, and the religion is known largely from colonial chronicles and archaeological remains
facts.followers: none counted: the Inca state was fully conquered by 1572, the Spanish moved against the worship of the royal mummies from 1559, and Pachamama is still honoured in Bolivian indigenous belief

t: The cosmos was divided into hanan pacha above, kay pacha where humans live and ukhu pacha and urin pacha within the earth, represented by the condor, the puma and the snake.
The Inca allowed conquered peoples to keep their own deities while making the cult of the Sun the official tradition of the empire.
Royal ancestors were mummified and consulted as advisors, and in times of great trouble the Inca practised human sacrifice, usually of a child (qhapaq hucha) or a slave.
dyk: The Cusco valley held 328 huacas, which were arranged along 41 or 42 radial pathways called ceques, all running out from the Coricancha, and the ritual duties for each shrine were recorded on quipus.
ev: In the early 1200s the Inca form the small city-state of Cuzco under Manco Capac, who builds a temple to the Sun God, called Inticancha, where the Coricancha stands
Under the ninth Sapa Inca, Pachacuti, the Inca begin the expansion that brings much of western South America into the empire, with the cult of the Sun as its official tradition
As many as 4,000 servants, court officials, favourites and concubines are killed on the death of the Inca Huayna Capac, one of the human sacrifices the Inca made
The Spanish begin the conquest of the Inca Empire, and on their arrival the Inca begin to hide the bodies of their kings and worship more secretly
Polo de Ondegardo, newly appointed Corregidor of Cuzco, hunts down the mummies of the Inca kings and sends them to the viceroy in Lima
The Taki Unquy movement arises in Huamanga, in the Peruvian Andes, calling for a return to the worship of the huacas and a rejection of the Christian god
The last Inca stronghold is conquered, and the Taki Unquy practice is estimated to have ended in the same year

sections.origins:
The Inca religion was a group of beliefs and rites related to a mythological system that evolved from pre-Inca times into the Inca Empire, or Tawantinsuyu. Its followers were polytheists, with local, regional and pan-regional divinities, and faith showed itself in every part of life, work, festivals and ceremonies. The Incas took over and institutionalised the religious practices of older Andean societies, most notably the Wari, Chavín and Nazca cultures. The empire was preceded by two large-scale empires, the Tiwanaku (c. 300–1100 CE), based around Lake Titicaca, and the Wari (c. 600–1100 CE), who occupied the Cuzco area for about 400 years. Aspects of Andean religion reach beyond the empire's former borders to the Mapuches and Huilliches of southern Chile, which has raised the hypothesis of an earlier spread of Andean religion from Tiwanaku.

In the early 1200s, under Manco Capac, the Inca formed the small city-state Kingdom of Cuzco. There Manco Capac built a temple to the Sun God, called Inticancha, in the current location of the Coricancha. The Incas had a great number of origin stories, which historians and scholars find hard to sort out; they often contradict themselves. Many place the beginning of life at Lake Titicaca. One legend collected by the chronicler Inca Garcilaso de la Vega has Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo sent by the Sun God, emerging from the lake.
sections.beliefs:
A theme of Inca mythology is the duality of the cosmos. Hanan pacha, the upper world, held the deities of the sun, moon, stars, rainbow and lightning; ukhu pacha and urin pacha were the realms of Pachamama, the earth mother, and of the ancestors and heroes of the Inca and other ayllus; kay pacha, where humans lived, lay between them. The condor stood for the upper world, the puma for the outer earth and the snake for the inner earth. In Andean thought, asymmetrical dualism holds that reality is built by different forces that need each other to be complete, one slightly stronger than the other. Camac is the life force that inhabits everything, living or dead, in different quantities, and places and objects with special energy were called wak'a: mountains, boulders, streams, battlefields, pottery believed to carry a deity.

Among the official deities were Viracocha, creator of humanity and everything else; Inti, the sun god, whose temple was the Coricancha, the Golden Enclosure; Illapa, who controlled weather, rain and lightning; Mamaquilla, Mother Moon and wife of Inti; Pachamama, the Earth Mother, protector of fields and crops; and Mama Cocha, Mother of Lakes. The Pleiades (Qollqa), mother of the stellar deities, marked the start of the agricultural year when they reappeared after 37 days unseen. Families sometimes kept household gods as small figures called chancas or conopas.
sections.texts:
No scriptures are recorded. Because of the Spanish conquest much direct evidence of Inca religion was lost, and modern historians rely heavily on colonial chronicles and on the archaeological remains of religious customs. The religion is therefore known largely through Spanish and colonial writers. The ritual duties of each shrine at Cusco were recorded on quipus, knotted string recording devices. Juan de Betanzos is cited for the Incas' turn to secrecy after the Spaniards arrived, and Garcilaso de la Vega for his sight of the embalmed kings at the house of Polo de Ondegardo.

One account of the origin has the creator god Wiraqocha Pachayachachic form giants at Lake Titicaca to see whether humans would work well at that size. Finding that they did not, he made them of his own size. These humans were hubristic and greedy and were turned to stone or other forms, some engulfed by stone or sea. The Creator then summoned a great flood to destroy all life except three men, who would later help create humans again. At a later point at Lake Titicaca he made the sun, moon and stars. The moon shone brighter than the sun, and the sun, filled with jealousy, threw ashes in her face to dim her. The Creator then spread out with two servants to call forth the people of every nation, from every mountain, crevice, cave and lake, before walking over the water into the west.
sections.spread:
From 1438 to 1533 the Incas incorporated a large portion of western South America, by conquest and by peaceful assimilation. The expansion began under the ninth Sapa Inca, Pachacuti, who reorganised the kingdom of Cusco into the Tahuantinsuyu. Religious traditions in the Andes varied among the different ayllus. The Inca generally allowed, or even took in, the deities and heroes of the ayllus they conquered, but they also brought their own gods to those peoples by building them into law, for instance by requiring sacrifice, and tried to combine their deities with conquered ones in ways that raised the status of their own.

The Inca leadership encouraged the sun worship of Inti and imposed its sovereignty above other religious groups, such as that of Pachamama, who had been worshipped long before the rise of the Inca. The Incas considered their king, the Sapa Inca, to be the son of the Sun. Locals were allowed to worship their existing beings, through pilgrimages, offerings and other rites, while still providing the sacrifices and offerings due to the Sun god. Some local traditions, such as the Oracle at Pachacamac on the coast, were officially venerated. The state religion was administrative and concentrated in Cusco, where a complex calendar set the state's festivals, holy days and major ceremonies.
sections.community:
Cusco's sacred geography held 328 huacas, objects, landmarks or shrines in and around the valley, arranged along 41 or 42 radial pathways called ceques that all began at the Coricancha. Ten royal kindred groups of Inca nobility, the panacas, served as the main priesthood in Cusco. They were responsible for the ancestral worship of dead emperors and the veneration of state deities, and were organised in two divisions of five, Hanan (Upper Cusco), north of the river, and Hurin (Lower Cusco), to the south. They took turns in ritual duties, offering sacrifices to the Sun, the Moon, Thunder, Viracocha and the Earth.

The Inca calendar had 12 months of 30 days, each with a festival, and a five-day feast at the end. The year began in December with Qhapaq Raymi, the first and biggest festival, when boys went through their puberty rites. Inti Raymi, at the June solstice, honoured the Sun god and ended with the ruler first to plough the earth.

Divination came before any action and nearly every rite was accompanied by sacrifices, usually maize beer, food or llamas, but occasionally virgins or children. Human sacrifice, usually of a child (qhapaq hucha) or a slave, is confirmed by archaeological remains on high mountain summits; specially chosen children were taken up to freezing peaks and left, either plied with alcohol or in some cases strangled. As many as 4,000 people were killed on the death of Huayna Capac in 1527.
sections.legacy:
Rulers were often mummified at death and worshipped within the palaces. Several times a year the mummies were seated in the order of their reigns in Cuzco's plaza, and in other months they were returned to their palaces and visited. The ruling Inca was expected to seek their advice on important matters. Not all mummies were honoured: Topa Inca Yupanqui's was burned and his bloodline killed for siding with Huascar in the civil war.

The Spanish began the conquest in 1532, and the Incas began to hide the bodies of the kings and worship more secretly. Polo de Ondegardo, appointed Corregidor of Cuzco in 1559, tried to stop what he saw as the Incas' idolatrous sins, found most of the mummified kings and sent them to the viceroy in Lima, where they stayed in a hospital for around 80 years before their whereabouts became unknown. Taki Unquy (c. 1564 to c. 1572), a movement that began in Huamanga, held that the wak'as would return and defeat the Spanish God. The visitador Cristóbal de Albornoz suppressed it harshly: its leader Juan Chocne and the other spiritual leaders were taken to Cusco to reject their beliefs in public, the women were imprisoned in convents and the kurakas were fined. The last Inca stronghold fell in 1572. Pachamama is still described as a source of fertility and abundance in Bolivian indigenous belief.

summary: Inca religion was the polytheist system of the Inca Empire, growing out of older Andean traditions and officially centred on the cult of the Sun, with Viracocha as creator and sacred places called wak'a. After the Spanish conquest began in 1532 the royal mummies were hunted down and the Taki Unquy movement was suppressed.
notes: Dates: none of the three articles says the religion ended. Start 1200 (circa) follows the Inca Empire article's 'early 1200s' for the Kingdom of Cuzco and its temple to the Sun God. End 1572 is the year the last Inca stronghold was conquered and the Taki Unquy practice is estimated to have ended; the Inca Religion article says Pachamama is still honoured in Bolivian indigenous belief, so the editor may prefer a different treatment.

Civil war: the Inca Empire article places the war of succession between Huascar and Atahualpa around the Spaniards' return in 1532 (one historian, Silva, is quoted as placing a battle in 1532 during it); the Inca Religion article gives no year for Topa Inca Yupanqui's mummy being burned, so the profile leaves that undated. Topa Inca Yupanqui's reign dates (1471-1493) are given as traditional historiography in the Empire article and were not used. The Pachacuti wawqi episode is undated in the sources and was left out of the key events; it was cut from the text.

Left out: the triad of Viracocha, Inti and Inti-Illapa and the theories on why Viracocha rose above Inti; Kon (Wakon); Mama Ocllo as regent; the story of Huascar's mother marrying his father's mummy; Garcilaso's quotation on the mummies; the Mamaquilla priestesses and the Coya as her daughter.

Faith map: Cusco, Lake Titicaca, Lima and Huamanga are named in the articles; coordinates from general geography. Lake Titicaca has no mark because no article dates anything that happened there. Taki Unquy's spread to Huancavelica, Lima, Cusco, Arequipa, Chuquisaca and La Paz is undated beyond the 1560s and is not drawn.
